statement: A permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 9\}$ is chosen uniformly at random. What is the expected number of elements $i$ for which $\sigma(\sigma(i)) = i$?

choices.misconception: I only counted the fixed points, where sigma(i) = i, and forgot that i can also come back in two steps through a swap.
I added the expected number of fixed points, 1, to the expected number of swaps, 1/2, but each swap contains two elements.
I treated sigma(j) as independent of sigma(i), so I used (1/9)(1/9) for each of the 8 values j other than i, giving 1/9 + 8/81 per element.
I added the fixed-point chance 1/9 to a sum of P(sigma(i) = j and sigma(j) = i) over all nine j, so the case j = i was counted twice.

hints: Write the count as a sum of indicators, one for each element.
By linearity, the answer is $9$ times the probability that one fixed element, say $1$, satisfies $\sigma(\sigma(1)) = 1$. Split by whether $\sigma(1) = 1$.
$P(\sigma(1) = 1) = \frac19$. For each $j \ne 1$, $P(\sigma(1) = j \text{ and } \sigma(j) = 1) = \frac19 \cdot \frac18$, and there are 8 such $j$.

solutions.reliable: Let $X_i$ be 1 when $\sigma(\sigma(i)) = i$. This happens when $\sigma(i) = i$, with probability $\frac19$, or when $\sigma(i) = j \ne i$ and $\sigma(j) = i$, with probability $\frac19 \cdot \frac18$ for each of the 8 choices of $j$. So $P(X_i = 1) = \frac19 + \frac{8}{72} = \frac29$, and by linearity the expected count is $9 \cdot \frac29 = 2$. The same computation gives $2$ for any $n \ge 2$. Transferable idea: linearity turns a messy count into one probability about a single element.
solutions.elegant: For a random permutation of $n$ elements, the element $i$ lies in a cycle of length $k$ with probability exactly $\frac1n$ for every $k$ from $1$ to $n$. Here $\sigma(\sigma(i)) = i$ means $i$ is in a cycle of length 1 or 2, so the probability is $\frac29$ and the expectation is $9 \cdot \frac29 = 2$.
